We need to create a cylindrical tin with no lid using $48\pi \,{cm}^{2}$ of sheet metal. What is the largest possible volume of the cylinder?
question.worked_solution:
First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $48\pi \,{cm}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}=48\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =48\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{48\pi -\pi {r}^{2}}{2\pi r} \\ h & =\frac{48-{r}^{2}}{2r}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}\times \frac{48-{r}^{2}}{2r} \\ V(r) & =\frac{(48r-{r}^{3})\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=\frac{(48-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \frac{(48-3{r}^{2})\pi }{2} & =0 \\ 48 & =3{r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =16 \\ r & =4\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=4$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(4)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=4$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=4\,\text{cm}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume, we substitute $r=4\,\text{cm}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V(4) & =\frac{(48(4)-(4)^{3})\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{(192-64)\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{2} \\  & =64\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the largest possible volume of the cylinder is $V=64\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$
